lead: A limit cycle is a closed path in the phase plane that nearby trajectories approach or leave. It is isolated, so it is not one orbit of a continuum. It gives a self-sustained oscillation of fixed amplitude and frequency, set by the system, not by the initial state. Relay-controlled furnaces, valve stiction and van der Pol circuits show it. In control, a limit cycle is often unwanted hunting; in oscillators it is the product. Describing functions predict its amplitude and frequency; the phase plane shows its shape and stability.
prereq: You need describing function analysis and phase plane analysis; common nonlinearities explains the relay and saturation shapes.

blocks.text: A limit cycle is a closed curve in the phase plane that is isolated: no other closed orbit lies arbitrarily close to it. The state moves round and round on the curve. A nearby state inside the curve and a nearby state outside may spiral towards it. Then the oscillation settles to a fixed amplitude and frequency, fixed by the system, not by the initial state. That is a stable limit cycle.
An unstable limit cycle repels nearby states; they spiral away. A semi-stable limit cycle attracts from one side and repels from the other. In each case the cycle is isolated.

Do not confuse it with a linear centre. The system ẍ + ω²x = 0 has a whole family of closed orbits, one for each initial amplitude. There is no isolation and no single amplitude. Do not confuse it with a forced response either. With a sine input the steady output has the input frequency; a limit cycle has its own frequency and needs no periodic input.
Some syllabi call a stable limit cycle self-oscillation, or hunting when it is unwanted, as in a valve that keeps cycling.

For a second-order autonomous system, ẋ₁ = f₁(x₁,x₂), ẋ₂ = f₂(x₁,x₂), the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem gives an existence test. Take a bounded region R in the plane. Suppose a trajectory enters R and never leaves. Suppose R contains no equilibrium point. Then the trajectory must approach a closed orbit in R. The limit set is a closed orbit.
The theorem needs the plane. It gives existence, not stability. A closed orbit may be stable, unstable or semi-stable; the theorem does not decide which. Check nearby trajectories separately.

The van der Pol equation is the standard example: ẍ − μ(1 − x²)ẋ + x = 0, with μ > 0. Here x is displacement and μ is a positive parameter. For small |x|, the term −μ(1−x²) is negative damping: energy is pumped in, so amplitude grows. For large |x|, the term becomes positive damping: energy is removed. The two effects balance on a closed orbit. The result is a stable limit cycle, and nearby phase-plane paths approach the closed curve.
A relay loop with a plant that has phase lag can show the same behaviour: a fixed-amplitude oscillation appears with no sine input.

The describing function replaces the nonlinear element by a gain N(A) that depends on the amplitude A of the sine at its input. The linear plant is G(jω). A limit cycle is predicted when the loop equation holds:

blocks.where: N(A) is the describing function of the nonlinear element at input amplitude A; G(jω) is the plant frequency response at frequency ω.

blocks.text: Rearrange to G(jω) = −1/N(A). The left side is a curve in the complex plane as ω varies. The right side is a curve as A varies. An intersection gives a candidate limit cycle: read ω from the G curve and A from the −1/N curve.

For a relay with output levels ±M, the describing function is N(A) = 4M/(πA). Here A is the amplitude of the sine at the relay input, not the relay output. Then −1/N(A) = −πA/(4M). On the complex plane this is a line along the negative real axis, moving left as A increases.

items: Write N(A) for the nonlinearity using the input amplitude A.
Plot G(jω) for ω > 0 and −1/N(A) for A > 0 on the same complex plane.
Find an intersection; record ω and A.
Treat it as a candidate. A separate stability check decides whether the oscillation is stable. The method is approximate because it keeps only the first harmonic.

blocks.text: The figure shows the relay case. G crosses the negative real axis at −1/6. The −1/N line meets it there, giving the amplitude and frequency computed next.

figure.caption: The Nyquist curve of G crosses the negative real axis at −1/6; the −1/N line meets it there, so the relay loop has a limit cycle.

spec.aria: The Nyquist curve of G meets the negative real axis at −1/6, and the relay describing-function line crosses it there, giving a limit cycle.

examples.question: A relay with output ±1 drives G(s)=1/[s(s+1)(s+2)] in a unity-feedback loop. The relay describing function is N(A)=4/(πA). Find the limit-cycle frequency ω in rad/s and the sine amplitude A at the relay input.
steps: Put s=jω. (jω+1)(jω+2)=2+3jω−ω². Multiply by jω: denominator = −3ω² + jω(2−ω²).
For G to be real and negative, the imaginary part is zero: ω(2−ω²)=0. With ω>0, ω=√2=1.414 rad/s.
At this ω, denominator = −3(2)+0 = −6, so G(j√2)=−1/6=−0.1667.
Loop condition: G=−1/N, so −1/6 = −πA/4. Thus πA/4=1/6.
A=4/(6π)=2/(3π)=0.2122. The relay output is ±1, but A is the input sine amplitude.
examples.answer: The limit cycle has ω=√2≈1.414 rad/s and relay-input amplitude A=2/(3π)≈0.2122.
examples.check:
import math
omega = math.sqrt(2)
G = -1/6
A = 4/(6*math.pi)
print(omega)
print(G)
print(A)

traps: In N(A)=4M/(πA), A is the amplitude of the sine at the relay input. The relay output level M is not A. Do not put 1 for A when the relay output is ±1.
A linear centre has a continuum of closed orbits with amplitude set by initial conditions. A limit cycle is isolated and has one amplitude and frequency set by the system.
A limit cycle is self-oscillation, not a forced response. Its frequency is not the frequency of any input sine.
Poincaré–Bendixson proves that a closed orbit exists. It does not prove that the orbit is stable; check nearby trajectories separately.
In 1+N(A)G(jω)=0, a sign slip gives +1/N instead of −1/N. For a relay, N(A) is positive, so −1/N lies on the negative real axis.

quiz.a: A limit cycle is an isolated closed trajectory in the phase plane. The system oscillates with fixed amplitude and frequency without an external periodic input.

quiz.q: Why is a linear centre not a limit cycle?
quiz.a: A linear centre has a continuum of closed orbits, one for each initial amplitude. There is no isolation and no single attracting or repelling amplitude.

quiz.q: A relay with N(A)=4/(πA) drives a plant whose Nyquist plot crosses the negative real axis at −0.25. Find the predicted amplitude A.
quiz.a: Condition: G=−1/N. So −0.25=−πA/4, giving πA/4=0.25 and A=1/π≈0.318.

quiz.q: A bounded region with no equilibrium contains a trapped trajectory. Does this prove a stable limit cycle?
quiz.a: No. It proves at least one closed orbit exists by Poincaré–Bendixson. Stability needs a separate check that nearby trajectories approach the orbit.

quiz.q: In the relay example the relay output is ±1. Why is A=0.212 and not 1?
quiz.a: A is the amplitude of the sine wave at the relay input. N(A) uses that input amplitude. The relay output is a fixed-level square wave and its level is not A.

quiz.q: For van der Pol ẍ−μ(1−x²)ẋ+x=0 with μ>0, what happens for small |x|?
quiz.a: For |x|<1, the damping term −μ(1−x²) is negative. Energy is pumped into the oscillation, so amplitude grows until nonlinear damping balances it on a stable limit cycle.

quiz.q: The curves G(jω) and −1/N(A) intersect twice. What must be done before calling either an actual stable limit cycle?
quiz.a: Each intersection is only a candidate giving an ω and A pair. Apply a stability test or a perturbation argument to see whether nearby amplitudes grow towards or away from the candidate. Not every intersection is stable.

beyond: Not for the exam. Limit cycles lead to bifurcation theory, where a parameter change creates or destroys a cycle, and to chaos in third-order and higher systems. The circle criterion and harmonic-balance methods give rigorous or more accurate tests. In industry, limit-cycle prediction is used for relay autotuning, valve stiction diagnosis and oscillator design. Search for van der Pol oscillator, describing-function stability, and the Poincaré–Bendixson theorem.
